cells.tense: Right now the pen is in your hand and you are naming what stands so it can be cleared.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you know has ended. Say out loud that it's over, then put it down and leave it down for a day.
cells.core:
You can say the shape of a thing. Not loudly — accurately — and that is what makes endings possible around you. You name what's finished without dressing it up or softening it, and because you do that, the room clears.

The structure you put on things serves what it holds. Nothing sags under it, nothing has to be managed around it. That's rarer than it looks, and it's the sign this is going well. What you're invited to feed next is a quieter kind of knowing, the kind you can't argue toward — you notice what's true and it lands. Say the clear thing once, then let it stand without another coat of paint. The clearing happens on its own after that. You don't have to keep declaring it. It's already named.
cells.sheetLine: You name what's over, and that's what clears the room.
cells.verb: naming the shape of something so it can stand and be cleared
cells.place: the point where what was has to fully end for what will be to emerge

cells.tense: You are bracing for an ending that hasn't arrived yet, writing it ahead of itself.
cells.ask: Write down every ending you're planning for. Circle one. The rest get no decision today — sit with the whole unordered list for ten minutes.
cells.core:
You're writing the ending before it's here. You see what needs to be cleared and you start declaring it early — naming it, framing it, getting the structure in place — so nothing catches you off guard. But you're authoring a page that doesn't exist yet, and the real ending keeps arriving late because you've already moved past it.

There's a shape of this where the structure serves what it organizes, where things make sense in your presence and no one has to brace. That doesn't require you to see further ahead. It asks you to sink deep enough into what's actually here that the pattern shows itself instead of one being laid over it.

So let what you're already planning to end sit unfinished. Ten minutes of not deciding will tell you more than another round of organizing.

cells.tense: You are standing at a doorway that closed behind you and it hasn't been named.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that one thing is finished. Then give one honest session to the work that comes after it.
cells.core:
Something has ended and you haven't said so. The room stays half-cleared because of that. Standing in a doorway that closed doesn't stop the closing — it just means you're the only one still there.

Naming things isn't what's hard for you. You can do it. What's gone quiet is the building that comes on the other side — the small, unglamorous craft that makes a new structure real. The offering stopped, and so did the work.

Structures that need to fall fall on their own, but only once you're standing on ground that's been prepared. Tell one person what you see is finished, then get back to the work that comes next. That's what moves you through the doorway and into something you can stand on.

cells.tense: The pen is down, but you are already writing the clearing in a room you haven't claimed.
cells.ask: Take one ending you've been describing as something that happened to you. Say 'I ended that' — out loud, once, where no one else can hear it.
cells.core:
You are already doing the clearing. You name what's finished, you let things fall, you make room — and then you describe it as though it happened on its own. The work is running. The credit isn't.

When structure serves what it organizes, things make sense in your presence, and people rely on that without seeing where it comes from. You've been giving that away for free, letting your own decisions pass as conditions you found yourself in.

The transformation you're in the middle of is the kind that trusts necessity — endings honored, renewal coming. But renewal gets trusted only when someone owns the ending. That someone is you. Say so, once, where it costs nothing, and then see what changes.

A reader could fairly say 'you don't know that about me,' so the cells describe the pattern in the moment, not the past. The ask still works if the read is wrong, because it's something worth doing about any clearing. The sentence that serves the writer is anything sweeping about 'the endings you've been avoiding' — cut it.
